meta.title: News Feed
meta.summary: Post updates and read a personalized home timeline (Twitter / Instagram style) at very high read volume.

functional: Post a short update with optional images
Read a home timeline of followed users, newest first
nonFunctional: Home timeline loads in < 200 ms p99
New posts may take a few seconds to appear (eventual consistency)
Reads must stay available even if posting is degraded

slos.name: Timeline speed
slos.sli: Timeline requests answered within the threshold, divided by all timeline requests, measured at the load balancer

slos.name: Timeline availability
slos.sli: Timeline requests not answered with a 5xx, divided by all timeline requests, measured at the load balancer

slos.name: Post freshness
slos.sli: Fanned-out posts whose id reached the followers' timelines within the threshold of being stored, divided by all fanned-out posts, measured by the fan-out workers from the post id's timestamp

slos.name: Posting works
slos.sli: POST /api/posts requests not answered with a 5xx, divided by all, measured at the load balancer. Kept separate so a posting outage never hides behind healthy reads.

alerts.when: Timeline errors burning the error budget 14 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
alerts.why: People cannot read their feed. This is the main product.

alerts.when: Timeline errors burning the error budget 3 times too fast (checked over 2 hours and 1 day)
alerts.why: A slow leak of failed reads that would use up the month's budget before anyone is paged.

alerts.when: Timeline requests over 200 ms burning the latency budget 14 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
alerts.why: Slow feeds drive people away even when nothing is failing.

alerts.when: Timeline requests over 200 ms burning the latency budget 3 times too fast (checked over 2 hours and 1 day)
alerts.why: Gradual slowdown, often a falling post hit ratio or more rebuilds than usual.

alerts.when: Posts reaching timelines later than 5 s burning the freshness budget 6 times too fast (checked over 30 minutes and 6 hours)
alerts.why: Timelines are going stale. Reads still work, so it does not page.

alerts.when: Post errors burning the error budget 14 times too fast (checked over 5 minutes and 1 hour)
alerts.why: Nobody can post; the feed slowly empties of new content.

alerts.when: Age of the oldest fan-out message above 30 seconds for 10 minutes, or any message in the dead-letter queue
alerts.why: Timelines go stale long before anyone sees an error, so this is the earliest warning.

alerts.when: Timeline cache memory above 85%, or evictions rising
alerts.why: Evicted timelines have to be rebuilt from the database, which is slow and expensive.

alerts.when: Post body hit ratio in the feed cache below 95% for 15 minutes
alerts.why: Every miss is a posts store read; at this volume a small drop multiplies load and cost on the store.

alerts.when: Fan-out worker failure rate above 1% for 15 minutes
alerts.why: Failed deliveries leave some followers without the post until the retry succeeds.

alerts.when: Posts store throttled requests above 0.1% for 10 minutes
alerts.why: Hot keys or exhausted capacity; reads fall back to slower retries.

signals.name: Age of the oldest message
signals.why: How far behind fan-out is, and so how stale timelines are.

signals.name: Evictions per second
signals.why: Shows memory pressure before timelines start missing.

signals.name: Throttled requests
signals.why: A viral post creates read spikes on a few keys.

signals.name: Post body hit ratio
signals.why: Decides how much of ~100M post reads/s at peak reaches the posts store.

signals.name: Timeline rebuilds per second
signals.why: Rises after a cache node loss or a wave of returning users; each one costs ~180 store queries.

signals.name: Posts and timeline loads per minute
signals.why: Business view: a drop in posts with healthy servers points at the app or upload path.

steps: Open a slow trace: is the time in the feed cache reads, the posts store or the celebrity merge?
Check the feed cache post hit ratio and timeline cache evictions.
Check posts store throttling: a viral post makes hot keys.
Check timeline rebuilds per second: many rebuilds mean many misses.
Count how many celebrity accounts the user follows: their posts are merged at read time.
Check the fan-out queue age first: it is the best single indicator.
Look at worker failures, retries and the dead-letter queue.
Check follower graph latency: fan-out pages through followers.
For celebrities, posts are not fanned out, so check the read-time merge path instead.

debug.symptom: A timeline cache node was lost
steps: Confirm the shard's replica was promoted; if it was, only seconds of fan-out writes are missing.
Watch timeline rebuilds per second and posts store throttling as users on that shard come back.
If the store throttles, lower the rebuild rate limit: slower rebuilds are better than failed ones.

nodes.label: DNS
nodes.description: Points the app hostname at the CDN

nodes.label: CDN
nodes.description: Serves images and video; passes API calls through uncached

nodes.label: WAF
nodes.description: Rule set attached to the CDN: managed rules, per-IP rate rules, bot control

nodes.label: Load Balancer (L7)
nodes.description: Public origin; accepts traffic only from the CDN

nodes.label: Fan-out Queue
nodes.description: PostCreated events; dead-letter queue after 5 failed deliveries

nodes.label: Fan-out Workers
nodes.description: Push new post ids into followers' timelines

nodes.label: Post Service
nodes.description: Accepts new posts and media uploads (~20k posts/s at peak)

nodes.label: Timeline Service
nodes.description: Builds the home timeline (~2M reads/s at peak, about 1,000 instances)

nodes.label: Social Graph Service
nodes.description: Who follows whom; caches each user's list of followed celebrities in memory

nodes.label: Feed Cache
nodes.description: Redis cluster sharded by key: per-user timelines (~800 post ids), hot post bodies, celebrities' recent post ids

nodes.label: Follow Graph DB
nodes.description: follows(follower_id, followee_id), indexed both ways; sharded by user id, read replicas for fan-out

nodes.label: Posts Store
nodes.description: Post bodies keyed by post id, plus an index by author for recent posts

flows.title: Post an update
flows.summary: Write path with fan-out on write: upload the image straight to storage, store the post once, then push its id into every active follower's cached timeline in the background.

steps.label: resolve feed.example.com
steps.detail: The app resolves the API hostname, which points at the CDN. The answer is cached on the phone and by resolvers.

steps.label: POST /api/media
steps.detail: Before posting, the app asks for an upload slot for the photo.

steps.label: inspect
steps.detail: The WAF attached to the CDN checks every request before it reaches the origin: managed rule sets, bot control and per-IP rate rules. Blocked requests get a 403 at the edge.

steps.label: sign upload URL
steps.detail: Signing is local (no call to storage): the URL allows one PUT of that size and type to one key, for 15 minutes.

steps.label: PUT image
steps.detail: The bytes go straight to object storage, so the Post Service never carries large files.

steps.label: POST /api/posts
steps.detail: The post references the uploaded image by id. The idempotency key makes a retried POST safe.
steps.payload:
POST /api/posts HTTP/2
Authorization: Bearer eyJ…
Idempotency-Key: 3c9e71

{ "text": "Shipping v2 today!", "media_ids": ["m_81f2"] }

steps.label: inspect
steps.detail: Same WAF rules; a per-account posting rate rule at the Post Service catches spam the per-IP rule misses.

steps.label: forward to origin
steps.detail: Writes are never cached; the CDN forwards them to the origin after the WAF check.

steps.label: route
steps.detail: Stateless Post Service instances sit behind the load balancer, which starts the trace that every later hop, including the fan-out message, carries.

steps.label: HEAD m_81f2
steps.detail: Checks the upload finished and belongs to this author before the post may reference it.

steps.label: PutItem post
steps.detail: The post id is a time-sortable Snowflake-style id (timestamp + machine + sequence), so ids sort by time without a global counter. The write is conditional on the idempotency key, so a retry cannot create the post twice.

steps.label: OK
steps.detail: The post is durable. If publishing the event below fails, the request fails and the client's retry finds the stored post and publishes again.

steps.label: publish PostCreated
steps.detail: Fan-out is slow for popular authors, so it happens off the request path.

steps.label: 201 Created
steps.detail: The author gets an immediate response.

steps.label: 201 Created
steps.detail: Back out through the edge.

steps.label: 201 Created
steps.detail: The client shows the post in the author's own timeline right away, even before fan-out finishes.

steps.label: deliver PostCreated
steps.detail: Workers scale with queue depth. A celebrity post is never fanned out, so no single post creates millions of writes. Delivery is at least once, so a post id can occasionally be pushed twice.

steps.label: GET followers(42) page 1
steps.detail: Followers are read in pages of a few thousand.

steps.label: SELECT follower_id
5,000 ids
steps.detail: Index on (followee_id, follower_id) makes this a range scan.

steps.label: followers page
steps.detail: Followers come back in pages; the worker writes one page while it fetches the next.

steps.label: LPUSHX + LTRIM ×N
steps.detail: Fan-out on write: one small write per follower, pipelined (not MULTI, since followers' lists sit on different shards). LPUSHX only pushes to a timeline that exists, so inactive followers, whose timelines expired after 30 days idle, cost nothing and get rebuilt when they return. Each list is trimmed to ~800 ids so memory stays bounded.
steps.payload:
LPUSHX timeline:1001 1857261298011340800
LTRIM  timeline:1001 0 799
LPUSHX timeline:1002 1857261298011340800
LTRIM  timeline:1002 0 799
…   (pipelined, grouped by shard)

flows.title: Read home timeline
flows.summary: Read path: precomputed ids from cache, merged with posts from celebrities that were deliberately not fanned out.

steps.label: inspect
steps.detail: The WAF also blocks scrapers paging through timelines faster than any person reads.

steps.label: private: pass through
steps.detail: Timelines are per-user, so the CDN does not cache them. It still serves every image and video in them.

steps.label: LRANGE timeline:1001 0 49
steps.detail: The timeline was built ahead of time by fan-out, so reading it is one memory lookup. Each read also pushes the list's 30-day expiry forward, so only idle users' timelines expire.

steps.label: 50 post ids
steps.detail: Sub-millisecond. This is why fan-out on write pays off: reads outnumber writes ~100:1. A missing list means the user was inactive; the miss flow rebuilds it.

steps.label: celebrities I follow
steps.detail: Hybrid model: accounts with more than ~100k followers are not fanned out, since one post would mean millions of cache writes. Their posts are pulled at read time instead.

steps.label: [nasa, elonmusk]
steps.detail: This list is small and cached in the Graph Service's memory.

steps.label: MGET posts + celeb recent ids
steps.detail: Hydrate the 50 ids into post bodies and read each followed celebrity's recent post ids, from the same cache cluster under different keys. At ~2M timeline reads/s, 50 posts each, hydrating from the posts store would mean ~100M item reads/s; the cache takes almost all of it. A celebrity's recent list is read by millions, so each Timeline Service instance also keeps those lists in memory for a few seconds, so one hot key cannot overload one shard.

steps.label: BatchGet the misses
steps.detail: Only cache misses reach the posts store; the results are written back to the cache.

steps.label: merge by time
steps.detail: Merge the two sorted lists by post id (which is time-ordered), dropping any id that appears twice, since fan-out is at least once and a late post can be pushed after newer ones. Then apply ranking if the product has one.

steps.label: 200 OK
steps.detail: Media URLs point at the CDN, so images load from the edge.

steps.label: GET on edge miss
steps.detail: Popular media is almost always a HIT at the edge; only the first view in each edge location reaches storage.

flows.title: Returning user (timeline cache miss)
flows.summary: Edge case: an inactive user's timeline was not kept, so it is rebuilt from the follow graph and recent posts, then cached again.

steps.label: GET /api/timeline
steps.detail: A user who has not opened the app for 40 days comes back.

steps.label: LRANGE timeline:2002 0 49
steps.detail: Fan-out skipped this user while inactive, so the list expired.

steps.label: who does 2002 follow?
steps.detail: The Graph Service reads the follower-keyed index, so this is one shard.

steps.label: SELECT followee_id
steps.payload: SELECT followee_id FROM follows WHERE follower_id = 2002;   -- 180 rows

steps.label: recent posts per followee
steps.detail: Queries the author index for each followee's latest posts, in parallel, and keeps the newest 800 overall. Slower than a cache read (tens of ms), which is why it is reserved for returning users.
steps.payload: Query posts_by_author: author_id = :f, post_id > :since, newest first, limit 20   (×180, parallel)

steps.label: RPUSH + EXPIRE
steps.detail: Store the rebuilt list so the next read is a hit and fan-out starts reaching it again. Rebuilds are rate-limited per cache shard so a lost cache node cannot turn into a stampede on the posts store.

steps.label: 200 OK
steps.detail: The returning user waits a little longer once; every later read is a normal cache hit.

notes.text: Fan-out on write makes reads cheap but writes expensive; fan-out on read is the opposite. The hybrid (write for normal users, read for celebrities) is the standard answer.

200M users × 800 ids × 8 bytes ≈ 1.3 TB of timeline ids, plus hot post bodies, Redis overhead and a replica per shard. Use a Redis cluster sharded by key (user id for timelines, post id for bodies); timelines expire after 30 days idle and fan-out skips missing ones (LPUSHX), so only active users cost memory. Fan-out writes are the real load: 500M posts × ~200 followers is ~100B list pushes a day, over 1M/s on average, spread across the shards. A separate post cache cluster is the usual next step when the two workloads need different sizing.

If fan-out falls behind, timelines are a few seconds stale but reads keep working. The queue absorbs bursts. Delivery is at least once, so the read path drops duplicate ids; a message that keeps failing goes to the dead-letter queue instead of blocking the rest.
Time-sortable ids (Snowflake style) avoid a central counter and let timelines merge and paginate by id.
Media is most of the bytes. Serving it from the CDN keeps the origin small.

About 40B follow edges (200M users × ~200), stored twice (by follower and by followee) and sharded by user id across several Aurora clusters, each a writer with a standby in another zone. Fan-out paging reads go to read replicas, since there is roughly one page query per post, ~20k/s at peak.

The WAF on the CDN stops bots, scrapers and floods at the edge; the load balancer only accepts traffic from the CDN, so it cannot be bypassed. Behind it, the data stores sit in the private data subnet, and the managed stores and queue (posts store, media bucket, fan-out queue) are reached through VPC endpoints rather than the internet.

questions.q: A celebrity with 50 million followers posts. Why is fan-out on write a problem, and what do you do?
questions.a: Writing one entry into 50 million timelines takes minutes and floods the cache and queue. Use a hybrid: fan out on write for normal accounts, but skip it for accounts above a follower threshold (~100k here) and merge their recent posts into the timeline at read time. Each celebrity's recent posts are read by millions, so they are served from the cache; readers pay a small merge cost and the system avoids huge write storms.

questions.q: The timeline cache loses a node. What do users see and how do you recover?
questions.a: Users whose timelines lived on that node get a cache miss. The timeline service rebuilds those timelines on read from the follow graph and the posts store's author index, which is slower but correct, and writes them back. Keep each cache shard replicated across zones so one node loss promotes a replica instead, and rate-limit rebuilds so a lost shard cannot cause a rebuild storm.

questions.q: How do you keep posts in a sensible order when they arrive late or out of order?
questions.a: Order by a time-sortable id (like a Snowflake id) generated when the post is created, not by arrival time in the fan-out queue. The cached lists are appended in arrival order, so the read sorts each page by id and drops duplicates (fan-out is at least once); a very late post can still land a page off, which feeds accept. Ranked feeds sort by score instead, but still need stable ids for paging.

questions.q: How does infinite scroll page through a timeline efficiently?
questions.a: Use cursor-based paging: the client sends the id of the last post it saw and gets the next N older ones. Offsets break when new posts arrive and get slower deep into the list. Keep only the most recent few hundred entries per user in the cache and fall back to storage for older pages.

questions.q: How would you store the follow graph so both "who do I follow" and "who follows me" are fast?
questions.a: Store each edge twice, indexed once by follower and once by followee, and shard both by that user id, so either lookup reads one shard. At ~40B edges that means several database clusters, with replicas taking the fan-out reads. For accounts with millions of followers, page through the follower list during fan-out rather than loading it at once.

questions.q: Where do photos and videos in posts go, and why not through the post service?
questions.a: Clients upload media directly to object storage with a short-lived signed URL from the Post Service, and the post only stores a reference after the service checks the upload exists. Viewers fetch media through the CDN. Pushing large files through the post service would tie up its workers and bandwidth for no benefit.
